lead: A pump is a machine that adds energy to a liquid and moves it from a low level to a higher level, or into a pressurised line. Every pump does this in one of two ways: a spinning impeller flings the liquid outward, or a moving boundary traps a fixed volume of liquid and pushes it out. The first family is rotodynamic, the second is positive displacement. The classification matters because the two families behave differently when the head changes, when the delivery valve is shut, and when the pump is started. Only a few universities teach this family tree in detail.
prereq: You need: pressure, gauge pressure and head from Unit 1, Fluid Properties and Fluid Statics. No pump theory is assumed.

blocks.text: A pump takes mechanical energy from a motor or engine and gives it to a liquid as pressure energy and velocity energy. The liquid enters at the suction side, where the pressure is low, so atmospheric pressure or a supply tank pushes water up the suction pipe. It leaves at the delivery side, into the delivery pipe. The head between these two sides is the head the pump must produce.

A rotodynamic pump has a spinning impeller with curved vanes. The vanes give the liquid a high velocity, and the casing turns that velocity into pressure. The liquid flows through continuously; nothing is trapped in a closed space.

A positive-displacement pump has a moving boundary — a piston, a plunger, a gear or a vane — that traps a fixed volume of liquid and forces it into the delivery pipe. Its ideal flow depends only on geometry and speed.

blocks.where: Q is ideal discharge in m³/s; V<sub>d</sub> is the volume trapped per revolution in m³/rev; N is shaft speed in rev/s. For a rotodynamic pump no such fixed V<sub>d</sub> exists, because the flow changes with head.

blocks.text: The figure shows the whole classification in one picture. Two branches, and each branch splits again.

items: Centrifugal: liquid leaves the impeller radially. Medium to high head with large flow; the workhorse of buildings and industry. See 7.2.
Axial flow: the impeller is a propeller and the liquid moves along the shaft. Very large flow at low head — irrigation and flood pumping.
Mixed flow: partly radial, partly axial, used where flow is large and head is moderate.
Reciprocating (piston or plunger): high pressure, small flow. See 7.7.
Rotary (gear, vane, screw): steady flow at high pressure, good for oil and viscous liquids.

blocks.text: The behavioural split matters more than the names. A rotodynamic pump's flow falls as the head rises, so it can run with the delivery valve shut. A positive-displacement pump pushes the same volume whatever the head, so shutting its valve raises pressure until a joint or pipe fails.

items: Deep-well (borewell) pump: a narrow, vertical multistage centrifugal pump. Several impellers sit one above the other on one shaft and each adds head, which a single impeller cannot do from deep down a Chennai borewell. The motor sits under water, below the pump.
Jet pump: a centrifugal pump on the ground with an ejector (nozzle and venturi) down the well. Part of the water is sent back down to draw more water up; used for shallow wells.
Gear pump: two meshing gears trap oil between the teeth and the casing. The usual lubricating-oil pump in a workshop.
Vane pump: sliding vanes in a rotor, used in hydraulic power packs, tractor hydraulics and power steering.
Hand pump: a village hand pump is a reciprocating plunger pump — small flow, high pressure from manual effort.

figure.caption: The pump family tree. Notice that the centrifugal pump sits under the rotodynamic branch, beside axial and mixed flow, while piston, plunger, gear and vane pumps all sit under the displacement branch.

spec.aria: A family tree splits pumps into rotodynamic and positive-displacement branches, with centrifugal and reciprocating examples.

examples.question: A pump for an office water tank has a rotating impeller with curved vanes. It delivers 20 L/s of water at 1450 rpm. (a) Place it in the pump family tree, using the volume handled per revolution as your reason. (b) Name a positive-displacement pump used as a small high-pressure hand pump.
steps: Convert the data: Q = 20 L/s = 20/1000 = 0.020 m³/s, and N = 1450/60 = 24.17 rev/s.
Curved vanes on a spinning impeller put the pump on the rotodynamic branch; the flow leaves radially, so the sub-branch is centrifugal.
Test it numerically. If the pump were a displacement pump, its trapped volume would be V<sub>d</sub> = Q/N = 0.020/24.17 = 8.28 × 10⁻⁴ m³ per revolution, that is 0.83 L per revolution.

A positive-displacement pump of a size that fits a building traps millilitres to a few tens of millilitres per revolution; a hand-pump cylinder holds a fraction of a litre per stroke. 0.83 L per revolution is far too large, so the pump cannot be positive displacement.
Part (b): the village hand pump is a reciprocating plunger pump — a plunger in a cylinder, worked by a lever.
examples.answer: The pump is centrifugal (rotodynamic branch): 20 L/s at 1450 rpm means 0.83 L per revolution, far beyond a positive-displacement pump of that size. The hand pump is a reciprocating plunger pump.
examples.check:
N = 1450/60
Q = 20/1000
V = Q/N
print(round(N,4))
print(round(V,6))
print(round(V*1000,4))

traps: Calling a centrifugal pump a positive-displacement pump. It is rotodynamic, and its flow falls as the head rises.
Starting a positive-displacement pump with the delivery valve closed. The pressure has nowhere to go; a centrifugal pump is safe at shut-off, a gear or plunger pump is not.
Treating suction and delivery as directions of rotation. They are the two sides of the pump: inlet and outlet.
Calling a submersible borewell pump reciprocating because it 'pushes' water up a long pipe. It is a multistage centrifugal pump.
Putting the gear pump on the rotodynamic branch. Gear and vane pumps are rotary positive displacement, because they trap fixed volumes between moving parts.

quiz.a: A pump in which a rotating impeller gives the liquid velocity, and the casing converts that velocity into pressure; the liquid flows through continuously and is not trapped.

quiz.q: What is the suction side of a pump?
quiz.a: The inlet side, where the pressure is low enough for atmospheric pressure or a supply tank to push liquid into the pump.

quiz.q: Why does the flow of a positive-displacement pump barely change when the head rises?
quiz.a: Each revolution traps and pushes a fixed volume V<sub>d</sub>, so Q = V<sub>d</sub>N depends on geometry and speed, not on head. Extra head only raises the pressure the pump works against.

quiz.q: A gear pump traps 12 mL per revolution and runs at 1440 rpm. Find its ideal discharge in m³/s and L/s.
A pump delivers 5 L/s at 2900 rpm. Find the volume per revolution and say whether a positive-displacement pump of that size is plausible.
quiz.a: Q = 0.005 m³/s, N = 2900/60 = 48.33 rev/s, so V<sub>d</sub> = 0.005/48.33 = 1.03 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 0.103 L per revolution. That is large for a small displacement pump, so the pump is more likely rotodynamic.

quiz.q: An apartment in Chennai must lift water from a 90 m borewell. Which pump from the tree suits it, and why will a single-impeller pump not do?
quiz.a: A multistage submersible centrifugal pump: several impellers in series on one shaft, each adding head, so the total lift is far more than one impeller can produce. It hangs under water, so suction lift is not a problem.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, pump selection follows published pump standards and manufacturer selection charts, where specific speed decides whether the machine is centrifugal, mixed-flow or axial. Multistage submersible sets are chosen by borewell diameter, depth and required head, and their impellers are often trimmed to match the duty point. Modern design uses CFD to shape impeller vanes and check cavitation before a casting is made. Useful search terms: 'API 610 pump types', 'affinity laws', 'multistage submersible borewell pump', 'CFD impeller simulation'.
